name: Isometric neck holds

angle.text: Users press the head against a hand, band or wall to build neck size and definition, which proponents link to a stronger-looking jaw and neck. Isometric neck work is studied for pain and strength; its effect on appearance has not been studied.

summary: Pressing your head against your hand to thicken the neck; studied for pain and strength, never for looks.
note: Clinical studies exist for neck pain and strength, not appearance.
currentQuick:
Isometric neck holds mean pushing the head against a hand, band or wall without moving it. Looksmaxxing communities discuss them as a free way to build neck size for a stronger-looking jaw and neck.
The research is on neck pain and sports injury, not on appearance. No study found has measured cosmetic neck change from the practice.
How it works: The neck muscles contract against resistance without the head moving; proponents expect repeated loading to build muscle size and strength.
Risks and caveats: The cervical spine is loaded during the exercise; published trials were supervised in clinical settings. People with chronic neck pain show reduced neck strength in studies, and pain can affect maximal-effort testing.
deepLead:
Isometric neck holds are exercises in which a person pushes the head against a resisting hand, a band or a wall without moving it, contracting the neck muscles while the head stays still. In looksmaxxing communities the approach is discussed as a way to build neck size and muscle definition, which proponents associate with a stronger-looking jaw and neck.
Published research on neck isometrics comes mainly from physical therapy and sports medicine rather than appearance research. Trials and measurement studies have examined isometric neck strength in people with chronic neck pain  and in athletes exposed to head impacts . A randomized trial in women with chronic neck pain compared intensive isometric neck strength training with lighter endurance training for pain and disability outcomes . No published study found in this review has measured cosmetic change in neck appearance from isometric holds.

name: Platysmaplasty (neck band surgery)

angle.text: Platysmaplasty is chosen to remove visible vertical neck bands and sharpen the neck contour, usually alongside a neck lift or facelift. The contour change is visible after healing. Evidence comes from surgical case series rather than controlled trials.

summary: Surgery that tightens the neck's platysma muscle to remove bands and sharpen the neck line; supported by surgical case series, not trials.
note: Real surgery with hematoma and other operative risks; evidence is mostly surgeon case series.
currentQuick:
Platysmaplasty tightens or reshapes the platysma muscle in the neck to reduce vertical bands and improve contour. It is usually done within a neck lift or facelift.
The published evidence is mainly surgeons' technique papers and case series; no randomized trials were found.
How it works: Surgeons plicate, cut or suture the platysma, for example in a corset pattern, so the muscle sits flatter and tighter beneath the skin.
Risks and caveats: Hematoma is the most common complication of related facelift surgery; persistent bands and contour irregularities have been reported with some techniques. It is performed by surgeons under anesthesia.
deepLead:
Platysmaplasty is a surgical procedure that modifies the platysma, the thin sheet of muscle across the front of the neck, to reduce visible vertical neck bands and improve the neck contour. It is usually performed as part of a neck lift or facelift, sometimes together with removal of submental fat .
Published literature consists mainly of surgeons' technique descriptions and case series. Techniques include midline plication, muscle resection or transection, and the corset platysmaplasty, which was described in 1990 to address persistent bands and contour irregularities seen after earlier methods . Hematoma is described as the most common complication of related facelift surgery . In looksmaxxing communities it is grouped with hardmaxxing procedures aimed at a sharper jawline and neck.

name: Cervicoplasty / Cervical contouring

chain: Neck skin, fat and muscle reshaped
angle.text: Looksmaxxing communities list cervicoplasty among hardmaxxing procedures for a cleaner neck and jaw transition; in aesthetic surgery it is part of neck rejuvenation. The contour change is visible after healing. Evidence is documented in surgical series with little controlled data.

summary: Surgical contouring of neck skin, fat and muscle; documented in surgical series, with little controlled evidence.
note: Evidence is surgeon technique papers and small series; the term also covers burn reconstruction.
currentQuick:
Cervicoplasty means reshaping the neck surgically, by managing skin, fat and sometimes muscle. It is used in aesthetic neck lifts and in reconstruction after burns.
The literature is technique descriptions, cadaver work and small series.
How it works: Surgeons remove or redistribute fat, tighten tissue and may redrape or excise skin, sometimes through a small incision under the chin.
Risks and caveats: Operative risks apply, and outcomes depend on skin quality as described in technique papers. No randomized trial data were found.
deepLead:
Cervicoplasty is a plastic-surgery term for contouring the neck by working on skin, fat and sometimes muscle. In aesthetic practice it is part of neck rejuvenation, and it also appears in reconstruction after burn contractures . Looksmaxxing communities group it among hardmaxxing procedures aimed at a cleaner neck and jaw transition.
The literature contains surgeon-described techniques, anatomical studies and case series. A 1997 report described a non-excisional anterior approach through a submental incision without removing skin, for patients with good skin contraction . Anatomical research has mapped fat compartments of the neck in cadavers . No randomized trials of aesthetic cervicoplasty were found.

name: Neck liposuction

angle.text: Neck liposuction is used to remove fat under the chin and along the neck, reducing a double chin and defining the jawline. The reduction in fullness is visible once swelling settles. Support comes from surgical case series; controlled trials are lacking.

summary: Suctioning fat from under the chin and neck; surgical case series support it, controlled trials are lacking.
note: Surgical risks include infection and contour irregularities; skin laxity affects results.
currentQuick:
Neck liposuction removes fat under the chin and along the neck through small incisions to define the neck and jawline. It is sometimes combined with muscle repair.
Evidence comes from surgeon case series, including a 320-case safety report; looksmax.org users describe the results as permanent.
How it works: A cannula attached to suction is passed through small incisions, usually under local tumescent anesthesia in published series, to remove fat.
Risks and caveats: Published risks include infection, contour problems and unfavorable results with poor patient selection. Skin retraction varies by site.
deepLead:
Neck liposuction, also called submental liposuction, removes fat beneath the chin and along the neck through small incisions using suction cannulas. It is performed to reduce a double chin and improve the neck and jawline contour, and is sometimes combined with platysma repair or other lifting techniques .
Published evidence consists mostly of surgeon case series and technique papers, including a retrospective analysis of neck liposuction and recontouring , a 320-case safety series using tumescent local anesthesia , and reports of complications . Skin retraction after suction lipectomy has been compared by treatment site in a 500-procedure study . On forums, users describe it as a permanent-fat-removal option for a sharper neck-jaw transition.

name: Neck fillers / skin boosters

angle.text: Aesthetic-medicine users inject hyaluronic acid fillers and skin boosters to soften horizontal necklace lines and improve neck skin quality. Smoothing is visible after treatment. Only registered trials were found in reviewed sources, with no published results.

summary: Hyaluronic acid injections for neck lines; only registered trials found, no published results reviewed.
note: Thin sources; clinician-administered injectable.
currentQuick:
Neck fillers and skin boosters are injectable treatments, typically hyaluronic acid, aimed at horizontal neck lines and skin quality.
The sources found are clinical-trial registrations, including a 26-person Restylane Refyne neck study, without published results to summarise.
How it works: A gel is injected into or beneath the skin by a clinician to add volume or hydration to creased areas.
Risks and caveats: Risks were not described in the sources reviewed. Fillers are administered by clinicians, and product regulation varies by country.
deepLead:
Neck fillers and skin boosters are injectable treatments, usually hyaluronic acid products, used to soften horizontal neck lines and improve neck skin quality. In looksmaxxing and aesthetic-medicine discussion they are an option for horizontal neck rhytides, sometimes called necklace lines.
Published human evidence found for this entry is limited to registered trials. A registered study (NCT04162496) evaluated Restylane Refyne for correcting horizontal neck rhytides in 26 participants and is listed as completed . Another registered study evaluated a hyaluronic acid-based filler, NCTF135HA, for anti-aging performance and tolerance in 146 participants . A registered trial combined Ultherapy with Sculptra for skin laxity .

name: Neck cream / retinoid for necklines

angle.text: Skincare-oriented users apply neck creams, some containing retinoids, to improve lines, laxity, crepiness and pigmentation on the neck and decolletage. Small product-specific studies report improvement in skin signs.

summary: Topical creams for neck lines and laxity; small product-specific studies report improvement in skin signs.
note: Studies are small and product-specific; contact allergy has been reported.
currentQuick:
Neck creams are cosmetic topicals, some containing retinoids or other actives, marketed for neck lines, laxity and pigmentation.
Published studies are small, product-specific trials of 12 to 16 weeks or so, reporting changes in skin appearance measures.
How it works: Ingredients such as retinoids, N-acetyl glucosamine or vitamin K2 are proposed to support skin matrix, hydration or cellular energy; the studies assess visible skin signs.
Risks and caveats: Irritation is a general concern for topicals, and a case of allergic contact dermatitis to an ingredient in a neck cream has been reported.
deepLead:
Neck creams are topical cosmetic products marketed to improve lines, laxity, crepiness and pigmentation of neck and decolletage skin; some formulations contain retinoids or other active ingredients. They are a low-intensity option discussed among skincare-oriented appearance communities.
Published studies are small, mostly manufacturer-linked cosmetic trials. An 85-woman study of a comprehensive neck cream applied twice daily for three months assessed texture, fine lines, laxity and hydration , and a 16-week clinical study evaluated a firming cream containing N-acetyl glucosamine on neck and decolletage signs of aging . Other reports include a nitric-oxide-enhancing neck cream , a randomized split-face/neck study of topical vitamin K2 (MK-7) , and a case of allergic contact dermatitis to a neck cream ingredient .

name: Tech neck correction

angle.text: Users apply exercises and ergonomic habits to undo forward head posture from screen use, which is said to shorten the visual neck and soften the jaw-to-neck transition. Symptoms of tech neck are studied; appearance effects of correcting it are not.

summary: Posture habits and exercises aimed at undoing a forward head from screen use; symptoms are studied, appearance effects are not.
note: No agreed definition of tech neck; no studies on jawline or facial appearance outcomes.
currentQuick:
Tech neck, or text neck, is a popular name for a forward-leaning head posture linked to long hours on phones and laptops. Correction covers ergonomic changes, posture awareness and strengthening or stretching of neck and upper-back muscles.
In looksmaxxing circles, it is discussed as a way to improve neck length and jaw definition in profile. Published research looks at pain and posture, not at changes to appearance.
How it works: Approaches described in clinical sources aim to strengthen deep neck flexors and scapular muscles, stretch tight posterior neck muscles, and reduce sustained screen-flexed positions with breaks and better screen height.
Risks and caveats: Posture exercises are generally described as low risk, though people with neck pain or neurological symptoms are usually advised by clinicians to seek assessment. Research on the topic is limited by the lack of a standard definition of text neck.
deepLead:
Tech neck, also called text neck, is an informal name for a forward-leaning head and neck posture associated with prolonged use of phones, tablets and laptops, and for the discomfort sometimes attributed to it. "Tech neck correction" refers to the exercises, ergonomic changes and posture habits that people use to reduce that posture. In looksmaxxing culture it is discussed mainly as a posture topic, because forward head carriage is said to shorten the visual neck line and soften the jaw-to-neck transition.
A 2023 scoping review of peer-reviewed articles found no consensus definition of text neck, which it described as a challenge for researchers and clinicians. Related clinical literature on forward head posture links it to long device use and to neck and upper-back pain, though the strength of that association differs by age group.
Evidence on appearance outcomes specifically is thin. Published work focuses on symptoms, posture measurement and skin changes on the neck, not on how posture correction alters facial or jaw appearance.

name: Neck stretches / chin tucks

angle.text: Users do chin tucks and neck stretches, sometimes adding weighted curls, to improve neck posture and, per forum claims, lift the hyoid area for a sharper profile. Chin tucks are used in physical therapy for neck complaints; appearance effects are unstudied.

summary: Deep neck flexor exercise used in physio for posture; forums claim it lifts the hyoid area, but no appearance studies exist.
note: Posture and pain use has clinical support; appearance claims have not been studied.
currentQuick:
Chin tucks pull the chin straight back to engage the deep neck flexors, and weighted versions are called neck curls. Physical therapy sources use similar exercises for forward head posture and neck pain.
Looksmax.org users say they improve neck posture and raise the hyoid area. No studies have examined those appearance claims.
How it works: The movement retracts the head over the shoulders and activates deep flexors such as longus colli. Forum believers say stronger flexors change how the chin and neck meet; this mechanism for appearance has not been tested.
Risks and caveats: Gentle exercise is generally low risk, but users report neck pain in some threads, and added weight raises load on the cervical spine. People with existing neck conditions are typically advised by clinicians to get assessed first.
deepLead:
Chin tucks are a head-retraction exercise in which the chin is drawn straight back, without tilting the head down, to engage the deep neck flexors. Neck stretches and chin tucks are used in physical therapy for posture-related neck complaints and are discussed in looksmaxxing forums as a way to improve neck posture, with some users adding weighted neck curls.
On looksmax.org, proponents say regular chin tucks make the neck look better in profile and, in their view, raise the hyoid bone area, reducing the look of a soft submental region. Some posters share before-and-after photos as evidence.
Clinical sources describe strengthening the deep neck flexors, including longus colli, as part of the management of forward head posture and neck pain. No published study located for this article has examined chin tucks for hyoid position, jawline definition or facial appearance.

name: Sternocleidomastoid (SCM) hypertrophy

angle.text: Looksmaxxers aim to build the sternocleidomastoid, the large muscle on each side of the neck, so the neck looks thicker and more defined. The muscle's anatomy is well described; deliberate hypertrophy for appearance has not been studied.

summary: Building the large side-neck muscles for a thicker look; anatomy is well described, hypertrophy for appearance is unstudied.
note: No studies found on SCM hypertrophy; thin source base.
currentQuick:
The SCM is the prominent muscle running from behind the ear down to the collarbone and breastbone. Looksmaxxing discussion treats building it as a way to get a thicker, more defined neck.
Anatomical sources describe the muscle but not training it for size, and no studies on its cosmetic hypertrophy were found.
How it works: The SCM rotates and tilts the head and flexes the neck, so training aimed at it is generally discussed as resistance work for those movements. This has not been studied for appearance.
Risks and caveats: No cosmetic-specific risks are documented. Neck loading is generally regarded by clinicians as requiring care in people with cervical spine problems.
deepLead:
The sternocleidomastoid (SCM) is one of the largest and most superficial muscles of the neck, running on each side from the sternum and clavicle up to the mastoid process behind the ear. In looksmaxxing culture, "SCM hypertrophy" refers to building these muscles so the sides of the neck look thicker and more defined.
Anatomy sources describe the muscle's attachments, nerve supply and function, but the Wikipedia article does not cover training or hypertrophy. No published study located for this article has examined deliberate SCM hypertrophy or its effect on appearance.

name: Neck-to-jaw angle (cervicomental angle) theory

angle.text: Forum frameworks hold that a cervicomental angle of roughly 105 to 120 degrees reads as more attractive in profile. Surgical literature describes the angle and how it changes with aging, but no study supports the specific range as a measure of attractiveness.

summary: A profile-angle idea (about 105-120 degrees) for a clean chin-to-neck line; surgery literature describes the angle, no study supports the number.
note: The ideal range is a community figure; no study located tests it.
currentQuick:
The cervicomental angle is the profile angle where the underside of the chin meets the neck. Forum theory says an angle around 105 to 120 degrees looks best.
Surgical literature describes widening of the angle as part of neck aging and covers treatments, but none of the studies found validate a numerical ideal.
How it works: The angle depends on chin projection, submental fat, platysma tone, skin laxity and the position of the hyoid and jaw. Surgical sources describe fat, muscle, skin and bone approaches.
Risks and caveats: As a measurement framework it carries no direct risk. Procedures that change the angle, such as injectables, fat removal or genioplasty, carry their own surgical and medical risks, discussed in the relevant articles.
deepLead:
The cervicomental angle is the angle between the underside of the chin or jaw and the front of the neck, seen in profile. In aesthetic surgery literature, aging of the neck is described as including a widening of this angle along with submental fat accumulation, loss of mandibular contour and prominent platysmal bands. In looksmaxxing frameworks, a "neck-to-jaw angle theory" holds that a sharper angle in a specific range, often quoted as roughly 105 to 120 degrees, reads as more attractive.
The angle is a topic in the plastic surgery literature on neck rejuvenation, which discusses combined approaches such as fat reduction, platysma work, injectables and devices. Studies located for this article describe treatments and anatomy; none establishes an ideal numerical range for attractiveness.

name: Collar and shirt choice for thick neck

angle.text: People with thick necks select collar shapes such as spread, point, button-down or mandarin and a suitable shirt fit to show the neck to its best effect. The change in look is immediate when worn. Collar types are documented; their effects on appearance have not been studied.

summary: Picking collar shapes and shirt fit to suit a thick neck; collar types are documented, effects on appearance are not studied.
note: Thin sources; no research on collar style and perceived neck size.
currentQuick:
This is a style practice: choosing collar shapes such as spread, point or button-down, and shirt fits, to flatter or emphasize a thicker neck.
Collar types are well documented, but no research was found on how they change the perception of neck size, and no community sources were available.
How it works: Collar shape frames the neck and jaw visually and affects how a shirt sits. Any perceptual effect on neck proportions is untested.
Risks and caveats: No health risks are documented. A shirt that is too tight at the neck is generally regarded as uncomfortable.
deepLead:
Collar and shirt choice for a thick neck is a clothing practice in which people select collar shapes and shirt fits to complement a larger neck, with the stated aim being to emphasize the neck. Shirt collars come in several standard shapes, including spread, point, button-down and mandarin styles.
No studies on how collar style affects perceived neck size or attractiveness were found, and the sources available are general descriptions of collar types rather than guidance for particular body types.

name: Fat-loss to reveal neck

angle.text: Users cut body fat to show sharper neck and jaw contours and reduce a double chin where excess fat is the cause. Where a double chin comes from bone structure rather than fat, sources note it usually needs surgical correction.

summary: Getting leaner to show neck and jaw definition; fat distribution is genetic and bone structure matters too.
note: No studies on neck-specific fat loss; spot reduction is not supported by exercise science.
currentQuick:
The idea is that lowering body fat makes the neck and chin area look more defined. A double-chin look can come from fat or from jaw structure.
Exercise physiology sources say fat cannot be burned from one chosen area, and where it comes off first is largely genetic. No neck-specific studies were found.
How it works: Overall fat loss from diet and activity reduces subcutaneous fat including around the neck, in an order that varies between people. Bony causes of a soft profile are not changed by fat loss.
Risks and caveats: No specific risks are documented for this practice; general risks of aggressive dieting are outside the scope of the sources found.
deepLead:
Fat loss to reveal the neck refers to reducing body fat so that neck and submental contours look more defined. Wikipedia notes that a double chin can arise from excess fat around the neck in some overweight people, or from a bony deficiency in people of normal weight, and that the bony form usually needs surgical correction.
Exercise physiology sources describe that fat is mobilized from the whole body rather than from the area being exercised, so spot reduction is not regarded as achievable by physiologists; where fat is lost first is strongly influenced by genetics. No study found in this research has tested fat loss specifically for neck or jawline definition.

name: Whey/creatine bulking for neck

angle.text: Looksmaxxers pair a calorie surplus, whey protein and creatine with direct neck exercises to add neck size and a stronger-looking frame and jaw area. The supplements are studied for muscle gain in general, not specifically for the neck.

summary: Using protein and creatine supplements alongside neck training to add neck size; the supplements are studied for muscle in general, not for the neck.
note: No studies examine supplements for neck size specifically; evidence applies to skeletal muscle in general.
currentQuick:
Some looksmaxxing communities pair neck training with a calorie surplus, whey protein and creatine monohydrate in the belief that a thicker neck improves the look of the jawline and frame.
The supplements themselves have research behind them for general muscle and strength gains, but no published trial has tested them for neck circumference or appearance.
How it works: Creatine raises muscle phosphocreatine stores and is reported to support high-intensity training capacity and, over time, lean mass when combined with resistance training. Early weight gain is largely water held in muscle. Protein supplements provide dietary protein for muscle repair.
Risks and caveats: A position stand cited on Wikipedia describes creatine as safe for healthy people, and a National Kidney Foundation review found creatinine rises within normal limits. Safety data are lacking for children and pregnancy, and supplement contamination has been reported in some surveys.
deepLead:
Whey and creatine bulking for the neck refers to the practice of combining a calorie surplus, whey protein and creatine monohydrate with direct neck exercises, with the aim of increasing neck muscle size. In looksmaxxing communities a thicker neck is often discussed as contributing to a stronger-looking frame and jaw area.
Creatine is the most widely studied sports supplement. Reviews report that it improves performance in short, high-intensity exercise and, combined with resistance training, can increase lean mass. These findings concern skeletal muscle in general; no published human study has measured the effect of whey or creatine on neck size specifically.

name: Gua sha neck / lymphatic drainage

chain: Stone scraped along neck and jaw
angle.text: Popularized on social media in 2021 and 2022, gua sha on the jaw and neck is used for debloating, a sharper jawline and skin rejuvenation. The tool-and-oil technique comes from traditional Chinese medicine; clinical evidence for these appearance aims is lacking.

summary: Scraping a smooth stone along the neck and jaw, popularized on social media for debloating and a sharper jawline; clinical evidence for these aims is lacking.
note: Short-lived puffiness changes are reported anecdotally; no trials on appearance outcomes.
currentQuick:
Gua sha is a traditional Chinese medicine practice in which a smooth tool is scraped over oiled skin. A gentler facial and neck version spread widely on TikTok in 2021 to 2022, where influencers promoted it for lymphatic drainage and skin rejuvenation.
In looksmaxxing circles it is discussed as a way to reduce facial puffiness and define the jaw and neck. No clinical studies of these appearance claims were found.
How it works: Proponents say light strokes move fluid toward lymph nodes and boost circulation. Traditional gua sha uses firmer strokes until red marks called sha appear. Wikipedia reports the practice lacks high-quality evidence of clinical benefit.
Risks and caveats: Traditional gua sha nearly always causes minor skin trauma such as redness or bruising; less common effects include burns, and rare serious harms have been reported. Infection is a concern with unsterilized tools or broken skin.
deepLead:
Gua sha is a traditional Chinese medicine practice in which a smooth tool, such as a ceramic spoon, coin or jade stone, is drawn across oiled skin. A lighter facial version applied to the jaw and neck became popular on social media in 2021 and 2022 for lymphatic drainage and skin rejuvenation.
Practitioners in beauty and looksmaxxing communities describe it as reducing puffiness and sharpening the jaw and neck line. Wikipedia states the practice lacks high-quality evidence of clinical benefit. No studies of neck or jaw appearance outcomes were found.

name: Kybella for neck/jowl

chain: Fat cells under chin broken down
Slimmer chin, neck and jowl line
angle.text: Kybella is injected to reduce fat under the chin for a slimmer, more defined chin and neck, with jowl and neck use being off-label. The reduction is visible after treatment. It was FDA-approved in 2015 for submental fat.

summary: Deoxycholic acid injections that dissolve fat under the chin; FDA-approved for submental fat, with jowl and neck use being off-label.
note: Approved only for submental fat; jowl use is off-label.
currentQuick:
Kybella is the brand name of deoxycholic acid, an injectable that the US FDA approved on April 29, 2015 for reducing moderate-to-severe fat below the chin. People seeking a sharper jawline or neck sometimes discuss it for the jowl area as well.
A generic version became available in the US in April 2021. A 2025 registered study examined patient satisfaction with combined face and neck treatments including Kybella.
How it works: When injected into submental fat it destroys fat cells, which the body then metabolizes over several months.
Risks and caveats: Treatment is clinician-administered and prescription-only. The Wikipedia page loaded for this entry does not detail adverse effects, so patients are referred to the product label and clinicians for the risk profile.
deepLead:
Kybella is a prescription injectable form of deoxycholic acid, made by Kythera Biopharmaceuticals and sold as Belkyra in some markets such as Australia. The US FDA approved it on April 29, 2015 for reducing moderate-to-severe fat below the chin, and a generic became available in April 2021.
When injected into submental fat it destroys fat cells, which the body then metabolizes over several months. Using it on the jowls or other neck areas is not part of the US approved indication; this article documents how the topic is discussed rather than recommending it.

name: Scalp micropigmentation

chain: Look of buzzed hair or density
angle.text: Scalp micropigmentation is used to give a bald or thinning scalp the look of a close buzz cut or greater density, and to conceal transplant and other scalp scars. The visual effect is immediate; it camouflages rather than regrows hair.

summary: A cosmetic tattoo of tiny pigment dots that mimics a buzzed head or denser hair; it camouflages rather than regrows hair.
note: No clinical studies cited; the pigment is semi-permanent to permanent and can be removed by laser.
currentQuick:
Scalp micropigmentation (SMP) is a non-surgical cosmetic tattoo that deposits pigment in the scalp to look like tiny hair follicles, giving the appearance of a close-cropped head or greater density. It is also used to conceal hair transplant scars and scars from burns or injuries.
In looksmaxxing forums it is discussed as an alternative to hair transplants or hair systems for men who prefer a buzzed look. Published clinical evidence was not found; Wikipedia's article relies on news and magazine sources.
How it works: Pigment is placed superficially in the epidermis and upper dermis, with color matched to the person's hair. Treatment typically takes three to four sessions of about two hours.
Risks and caveats: Poor technique can produce an unnatural hairline. Practitioners may patch-test for ink allergy. Wikipedia reports that the result is permanent but can be removed by laser, and notes that its statement about no scientific data on side effects lacks a citation.
deepLead:
Scalp micropigmentation (SMP), also called a hair tattoo, is a non-surgical cosmetic tattoo that makes a bald or thinning scalp look like a close buzz cut or gives the impression of more density. It can also conceal hair transplant scars and burn or other scars on the head.
Pigment is deposited into the scalp to mimic tiny hair follicles, more superficially than a traditional tattoo. The article on Wikipedia cites no clinical studies; its sources are news and magazine pieces from 2012 onward. In looksmaxxing forums it is compared with hair transplants and hair systems.

name: PRP for hair

angle.text: Users get scalp injections of their own platelet-rich plasma for androgenetic alopecia or alopecia areata, as an option alongside or instead of minoxidil or finasteride. Small trials report gains, but the research base is limited and protocols vary.

summary: Scalp injections of a person's own platelet concentrate for hair loss; small trials report gains, but the research base is limited and protocols vary.
note: Off-label use; preparation devices need FDA clearance but PRP itself is not regulated as a drug.
currentQuick:
Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) is made by centrifuging a person's own blood to concentrate platelets, which release growth factors. For hair, it is injected into the scalp, usually in repeated sessions, as a treatment for androgenetic alopecia and sometimes alopecia areata.
Small randomized and pilot studies, plus registered trials, have examined it; Wikipedia notes its benefits remain disputed overall and that reported efficacy varies with factors such as number of sessions and preparation method.
How it works: Platelets are concentrated to about three to five times normal levels and are thought to release growth factors and cytokines that influence healing and possibly follicle activity.
Risks and caveats: Adverse effects are generally low in trials. In April 2024 the CDC reported HIV infections in three women who received PRP with microneedling at an unlicensed spa that reused equipment. Use for hair is off-label.
deepLead:
Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) is a concentrate of plasma protein from a person's own blood, in which red blood cells are removed and platelets retained. Platelets are thought to release growth factors and cytokines that aid healing, though Wikipedia says its benefits remain disputed. For hair loss, PRP is injected into the scalp as an option for androgenetic alopecia and alopecia areata, sometimes discussed as an alternative or addition to minoxidil or finasteride.
A double-blind, placebo-controlled pilot in women with female androgenetic alopecia compared PRP with saline injections, measuring hair count and hair mass index. A prospective study reported that repeated PRP scalp injections improved patient-reported quality of life using the HAIRDEX 48 tool. Wikipedia says PRP was first considered for androgenic alopecia and alopecia areata around 2006.

name: Exosome hair therapy

angle.text: Clinics and cosmetic brands offer exosome serums, microneedling and injections said to prompt dormant follicles to regrow hair. Only small registered trials exist so far, so the regrowth claim remains largely untested.

summary: Scalp serums or injections of cell-derived vesicles sold as follicle revivers; only small registered trials so far.
note: FDA describes exosome products as unapproved drugs; no peer-reviewed hair outcomes cited.
currentQuick:
Exosome hair therapy applies vesicles released by cultured cells, often umbilical cord stem cells, to the scalp as a serum, via microneedling, or by injection. Providers say the vesicles signal to follicles and support regrowth.
Small trials are registered for androgenetic alopecia and thinning hair, but this article cites registrations rather than published results, so efficacy is not established.
How it works: Exosomes are proposed to carry proteins and nucleic acids that mediate cell-to-cell signalling; Wikipedia notes functional RNA transfer in mammals is not firmly shown. Hair-specific mechanisms are claimed by providers rather than demonstrated in cited work.
Risks and caveats: The FDA has said exosome products are drugs requiring premarket approval and has reported advisories about noncompliant marketing and injuries in Nebraska (not hair-specific). Hair-specific safety data are not available in the cited sources.
deepLead:
Exosome hair therapy refers to scalp treatments, applied as serums, through microneedling or by injection, that contain exosomes: nanometre-scale vesicles released by cells that carry proteins, lipids and nucleic acids. Clinics and cosmetic brands that offer it say the vesicles, usually derived from cultured mesenchymal stem cells such as umbilical cord cells, signal to dormant follicles and prompt regrowth. 
Exosomes are a real and active subject of biomedical research, but their use in hair loss is at an early stage. Registered trials exist for androgenetic alopecia and self-perceived thinning, mostly small (about 15 to 100 participants) and many labelled early phase or not applicable.  No peer-reviewed efficacy results from these trials are cited here, so the effectiveness of the approach has not been established in the sources available.
In the United States, the FDA has stated that exosome products are drug products that require premarket approval, and Wikipedia notes advisories about noncompliant marketing.

name: Stem cell hair therapy

angle.text: Clinic treatments inject fat-derived, follicle-derived or donor cells, or cell-derived extracts, into the scalp to slow hair loss or promote regrowth. Small trials are registered and no approved product exists.

summary: Clinic injections of fat-derived or follicle-derived cells for hair regrowth; small trials registered, no approved product.
note: Wikipedia reports regulator action against unapproved stem-cell clinics; costs often run $10,000+.
currentQuick:
Stem cell hair therapy covers procedures that place cells or cell-derived products into the scalp to counter hair loss. Sources include a patient's fat, hair follicle cells or donor mesenchymal cells.
Small trials are registered, but no published results are cited here and no such treatment is FDA-approved for hair loss.
How it works: Proponents say the cells secrete growth factors that stimulate dormant follicles. In the cited sources this is a proposed mechanism under study in early trials.
Risks and caveats: Wikipedia reports FDA and FTC action against clinics selling unapproved stem-cell treatments, and serious infections after some cell products in 2021 (not hair-specific). Costs are commonly high and insurance typically does not cover them.
deepLead:
Stem cell hair therapy is an umbrella term for treatments that inject or apply cells, or products derived from cells, to the scalp in order to slow hair loss or promote regrowth. Variants include adipose-derived (fat) stem cell preparations, stromal vascular fraction, cells cultured from a patient's own hair follicles, donor mesenchymal stem cells, and cell-conditioned extracts or secretomes. 
Clinics that offer such procedures say the cells release growth factors that reawaken miniaturised follicles. Researchers are testing these ideas in small registered trials, many of them early phase or without a control comparison.  Wikipedia notes that as of 2024 the only FDA-approved stem-cell therapy is hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, and that hundreds of US clinics have sold mostly unproven stem-cell treatments, with the FDA and FTC taking enforcement action against some.

name: Hair cloning

angle.text: Hair cloning is a long-promised approach in which follicle cells are multiplied in the laboratory and implanted, aiming to remove the donor-supply limit of hair transplants. It remains in animal and lab research rather than clinical use.

summary: Multiplying follicle cells in a lab to grow unlimited hair is a long-promised idea that remains in animal and lab research.
note: No approved product; commercial programmes have closed.
currentQuick:
Hair cloning would take cells from healthy follicles, multiply them in culture, and implant them to make new hair follicles, avoiding the donor limits of transplantation.
Per Wikipedia, it is in early stages, with milestones in mice and several company programmes ended.
How it works: Follicle-inducing cells such as dermal papilla cells, or iPSC-derived cells, are expanded in the lab and implanted to interact with scalp epithelium and form follicles.
Risks and caveats: No approved treatment exists, so no human safety record is cited. Obstacles listed include inconsistent hair direction, thin follicles and cycling shown only in mice.
deepLead:
Hair cloning, also called hair multiplication or follicle neogenesis, is a proposed regenerative approach to hair loss in which a small number of cells from healthy follicles, such as dermal papilla cells, are multiplied in the laboratory and then implanted into balding scalp to form new follicles.  It is aimed at overcoming the main limit of hair transplantation, a finite supply of donor hair.
As of the sources consulted, hair cloning remains experimental. Wikipedia describes the field as in its early stages, with parts of the process shown at small scale, mostly in animals, and no approved product.  Companies including Intercytex and Aderans ended their programmes, and Stemson Therapeutics closed in December 2024.
